paras.say: In nineteen seventy-two, West Germany threw a party for the whole world.
It was meant to bury a memory.
The last time Germany had hosted the Summer Olympics was Berlin, nineteen thirty-six. Hitler's Games.
So Munich would be the opposite. The Cheerful Games. Soft colours... a dachshund mascot... and guards in light blue, most of them unarmed.
Then, at about four thirty in the morning, on the fifth of September... eight men climbed the fence into the Olympic Village.
Athletes coming home from a night out helped them over. They thought they were fellow Olympians.
They went to Connollystrasse thirty-one. The building where Israel's team was staying.
Wrestling coach Moshe Weinberg fought back, and was killed. So was weightlifter Yossef Romano. Nine more were taken hostage.
The gunmen, from a Palestinian group called Black September, demanded the release of more than two hundred prisoners held in Israel.
And the world was watching. By some estimates, nine hundred million people.
Police crept across the rooftops to storm the building... live on television. The gunmen were watching the same broadcast. The raid was called off.
That night, hostages and captors were flown by helicopter to Fuerstenfeldbruck air base, west of Munich.
paras.display: That night, hostages and captors were flown by helicopter to Fürstenfeldbruck air base, west of Munich.

paras.say: The rescue plan was waiting. Five police snipers. No telescopic sights. No night vision. No radios. And they had been told there were five gunmen. There were eight.
The officers hidden on the waiting plane decided the plan was suicide, and left.
The shooting lasted more than an hour. By midnight, all nine hostages were dead. So was a German police officer, Anton Fliegerbauer.
Early reports said the hostages had been saved. Then, after three in the morning, ABC's Jim McKay told America... They're all gone.
The Games stopped for thirty-four hours. Eighty thousand people filled the stadium for a memorial.
Then the head of the Olympic Committee, Avery Brundage, told them: the Games must go on.
It took fifty years for Germany to apologise. In twenty twenty-two, its president called it a triple failure. The families received twenty-eight million euros.
Munich was meant to make the world forget Berlin. Instead... it gave the world eleven names to remember.
